Confirmed: 1−w = 0, 0.0556, 0.1667, 0.3611 (rotor1); rotor2 = 0, 0.0588, 0.1765, 0.3529. Nice: two rotors with very different intrinsic widths (14.4 vs 3.4) and different stop angles share 1−w to ~2%. That's the "shared w(L)" fact.

Now Ω_est values: with ell = 1.577, 3.154, 4.731:
- 1/(1−w) = 18.0, 6.0, 2.77
- Ω = k_d L²cos²θ/(2 k_c ell²) with θ=20°, k_d L²=7.54, 2k_c=0.14:
  ell=1.577: 7.54*0.883/(0.14*2.487)=6.66/0.348=19.1 → ratio 19.1/18.0 = 1.06
  ell=3.154: 6.66/1.393=4.78 → ratio 0.80
  ell=4.731: 6.66/3.134=2.13 → ratio 0.77
So Ω ≈ 0.8–1.1 × 1/(1−w). Hmm the coincidence is suggestive but note both are ∝ 1/ell² by construction and 1/(1−w) is ∝ roughly ell^1.8-2.2/... i.e. the coincidence partly follows from both being ∝ 1/ell²; the prefactors happen to be ~1. That weakens the "measurement" claim: it's not independent evidence, since I chose the normalization k_c=0.07, L, θ to make it. But the fact that the prefactor is O(1) with no tuning (given k_d=0.19, k_c=0.07, L=6.3, θ≈20°) is interesting. Still, honest: the coincidence is guaranteed to order-of-magnitude if both quantities are monotone in ell² and the only dimensional ratio available is k_c/k_d ~ 0.37. Indeed: 1−w ∝ (k_c/k_d)(ell/L)²·f and 1/Ω ∝ (k_c/k_d)(ell/L)²/f'. So both = (k_c/k_d)(ell/L)² × O(1). At ell=4.731: (0.07/0.19)(22.38/39.69)=0.368*0.564=0.208; 1−w=0.361 → f≈1.7; 1/Ω=0.47 → f'≈2.3. So indeed both are the same dimensionless group (k_c/k_d)(ell/L)² times O(1) factors. That's the real insight: there is only ONE dimensionless group governing loop-width shrinkage and visibility, namely κ = (k_c/k_d)(ell/L)² (times geometry), so w and Ω cannot be independent knobs — 1−w ≈ 1.7κ and 1/Ω ≈ 2.3κ. This is a conceptual statement, not an empirical coincidence: dimensional analysis + both mechanisms being "coupling torque vs drive stiffness".

That's a good, honest development: rather than claiming a numerical coincidence, note that both 1−w and 1/Ω reduce to the same dimensionless group κ=(k_c/k_d)(ell/L)², so the clamped table's width column and the visibility criterion are two readings of one group. Consequence: (i) you cannot increase loop shrinkage without simultaneously approaching silence (Ω→1) — a *trade-off relation*, i.e., the apparatus has a one-parameter family; (ii) to test the Ω criterion you must vary k_d alone (holding geometry), because varying ell moves both readings together; the case service reports unknown whether k_d was constant across the table, so the four-point table cannot separate them; (iii) F4's exponent finding (1.58 vs 2) is then a *deviation of the geometry factor* f(θ, stops) at small ell — and maybe indicates the small-angle/point-mass model breaks at ell small relative to spring rest length.

Wait: is κ the right group? 1−w = (coupling torque diff)/(drive torque sensitivity): numerator ∝ k_c ell² δ(stop angles); denominator ∝ k_d L² cos²θ... Hmm careful: drive torque ≈ k_d (γ − ...) L cosθ, dT_d/dγ = k_d L cosθ (not L²). Let me redo. In my Ω I wrote k_d L²cos²θ as a torsional stiffness (torque per radian), since γ is the drive rod displacement mapped to angle: T_d = k_d L (γ_displacement...) Actually torque from a spring attached at distance L to a translating rod: T = k_d L cosθ × (γ − L sinθ...) so ∂T/∂θ = −k_d L² cos²θ. So torsional stiffness = k_d L²cos²θ ✓. And ∂T/∂γ = k_d L cosθ. Threshold shift δγ = δT_c/(k_d L cosθ) ∝ k_c ell² δθ/(k_d L cosθ)... and width ratio change ∝ (coupling curvature)/(drive torsional stiffness) = k_c ell²/(k_d L²cos²θ) = 1/Ω. Yes! So 1−w ∝ k_c ell²/(k_d L²cos²θ) = 1/Ω exactly — same group, and to first order w = 1 − 1/Ω + O(1/Ω²)? Check: at ell=4.731, 1/Ω=0.47 but observed 1−w=0.361; at ell=3.154, 1/Ω=0.209 vs 0.167; at 1.577: 0.052 vs 0.056 (!). So the relation 1−w ≈ 1/Ω holds within ~25% for the two larger ell and 7% at small ell, with a systematic ~0.8 factor. Great: 1−w = c/Ω with c ≈ 0.77–1.06. That's essentially "1−w = 1/Ω" up to an O(1) factor. Good—and this is now a *derived relation*, not a coincidence: both are the same ratio of coupling stiffness to drive stiffness. The prefactor follows from the number of coupling springs and the stop-angle geometry.

This is a solid domain-scientist contribution: "the loop-width column is the dimensionless stiffness ratio κ = k_c ell²/(k_d L²cos²θ) ≈ 1/Ω^vis, so loop shrinkage and visibility are not independent; the clamp table's width column already measures the stiffness ratio the Ω criterion needs in the dead-load limit." And a concrete consequence: with only geometry varied (ell), the table has a one-parameter family: κ ≈ 0.056, 0.167, 0.361 for the last three cells; Ω_vis = 1/κ ≈ 18, 6, 2.8 — all >1, so no silent cell observed. Silence would need κ→1, i.e. ell ≈ 4.731×sqrt(1/0.361×...)... Let's estimate: κ(ell) ≈ 1.7 (k_c/k_d)(ell²/L²)? At ell=4.731: (0.07/0.19)*(22.38/39.69)=0.208, observed 0.361 → factor 1.74. So κ=1 at ell² = L²(k_d/k_c)/1.74 = 39.69*(2.714)/1.74 = 61.9 → ell=7.87 cm, beyond w/2=7.6 cm pivot spacing — i.e., the silent cell is *geometrically unreachable* in pair_A with the current springs! That's a concrete conditional consequence: silence (w=0, Ω=1) cannot be reached by pushing ell to its geometric limit with the installed k_c/k_d; reaching it requires a softer drive spring (k_d reduced ~5×) rather than larger ell. That's a nice, checkable design statement (hypothetical, learning example). And it explains why all recorded pair_A cells show visible jumps — a nontrivial reading of the table.

Let's double-check: κ=1 → 1.74*(0.07/0.19)*(ell²/39.69)=1 → ell² = 39.69*0.19/(0.07*1.74) = 39.69*0.19/0.1218 = 61.9 → ell=7.87. Yes. And ell is bounded by w=15.2 cm pivot spacing, so ell max ~7.6 (attachments can't exceed pivot distance), so κ_max ≈ 1.74*0.368*(57.8/39.69)=0.93 — just below 1! Wow: the silent cell is essentially at the geometric limit — 0.93 vs 1. So pair_A at ell→w/2 would be right at the transition. That's a striking conditional statement: the apparatus sits within a factor ~1.1 of the branch-coalescence threshold at its widest possible mounting distance; the observed 1.2 cm silence... hmm, "silence band" earlier. Interesting but speculative; label as learning estimate.

Now, what about peer's R/P axes? My contribution: the Ω/κ relation locates the continuous-branch effect on the *width* coordinate, i.e., P axis, and — importantly — it gives a reason why R is untouched: as κ→1 the hysteron's loop width →0, so it degenerates into a *monotone* element, which trivially has RPM (single-valued, no stack). Degeneration cannot create multi-periodicity; it deletes a symbol from the alphabet. So R intact. That answers shared question (e) with a *reason*, not just placement: width collapse is a limiting process that removes hysteresis rather than scrambling it; therefore it belongs to P (and actually to the trivial end of P), and R is unaffected. Nice.

But caution: does a nearly-degenerate hysteron with very small loop width plus coupling create frustration effects? Small-width hysterons can be more easily "flipped" by neighbors, i.e., avalanches more likely → P axis scrambled; but R? Peer says R needs frustration + region + window. A near-zero-width hysteron could make the network's effective coupling stronger relative to its own gap → latch avalanches → but still RPM if no frustration. Fine.
